\|T_{R}(g)-T_{R}(h)\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}&\leq K(1+C)\|(\chi_{R}-1)Q\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\|g-h\|_{\mathcal{X}_{s}}\end{aligned},
with K independent of C and R . Fixing C>2K and then taking R large makes T_{R} preserve this ball and have Lipschitz constant less than one; its arguments also lie in the domain of \Phi . Its solution satisfies P_{\mathrm{un}}((\chi_{R}-1)Q+g_{R})=\Phi(P_{\mathrm{st}}((\chi_{R}-1)Q+g_{R})) , so v(0)=(\chi_{R}-1)Q+g_{R} lies on the constructed graph and Q+v(0)=\chi_{R}Q+g_{R}\in C_{c}^{\infty} . Since F is fixed and finite-dimensional, g_{R}\to 0 in every H^{m} .
∎
Proof of Theorem 1.1.
Fix 0<\mu<\omega and choose localized data from Proposition 4.8. By (57) and (70), V=Q+v is uniformly bounded and
\|V(\tau)-Q\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim e^{-\mu\tau}.
Its initial datum is smooth and compactly supported. Rewriting the Duhamel formula for v relative to S_{0} and using (63) shows that V solves (51). Higher regularity persists, and the tame product estimate yields, for every integer m\geq 3 for which V(0)\in H^{m} ,
(74)
\|V(\tau)\|_{H^{m}}\leq\|V(0)\|_{H^{m}}\exp\left(\left(\frac{d}{4}-\frac{1}{p-1}\right)\tau+C_{m}\int_{0}^{\tau}\|V(\sigma)\|_{\infty}^{p-1}\,d\sigma\right).
Consequently, a bounded L^{\infty} norm prevents finite-time breakdown and propagates all initial Sobolev regularity. Uniqueness and (74) therefore give V\in C([0,\infty);H^{m}) for every integer m\geq 0 . For any T>0 , undoing (4) gives
u(t,x)=(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}e^{-i\Omega\tau}V(\tau,y).
Therefore,
\left\|(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}e^{i\Omega\tau}u\left(t,\sqrt{T-t}\,\cdot\right)-Q\right\|_{\infty}=O((T-t)^{\mu}),
and hence
\|u(t)\|_{\infty}=(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\left(\|Q\|_{\infty}+O((T-t)^{\mu})\right).
The resulting solution lies in C([0,T);H^{m}) for every m , with smooth compactly supported initial data. Since Q(0)=A>0 , we have \|Q\|_{\infty}>0 , and T is its maximal time of existence. Finally, (54) gives |Q(r)|\gtrsim r^{-2/(p-1)} for r\geq 1 . Therefore,
\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|Q(x)|^{\frac{d(p-1)}{2}}\,dx\gtrsim\int_{1}^{\infty}r^{d-1}r^{-d}\,dr=\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{dr}{r}=\infty,
so Q\notin L^{d(p-1)/2} . As V(\tau)\to Q pointwise, Fatou’s lemma gives \|V(\tau)\|_{L^{d(p-1)/2}}\to\infty . Sobolev embedding and scaling invariance yield
\|u(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{c}}}\gtrsim\|u(t)\|_{L^{\frac{d(p-1)}{2}}}=\|V(\tau)\|_{L^{\frac{d(p-1)}{2}}}\longrightarrow\infty,
which completes the proof.
∎

Abstract.
We consider the mass supercritical (NLS) i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+u|u|^{p-1}=0 in dimension d\geq 1 in the mass-supercritical range 0<s_{c}=\frac{d}{2}-\frac{2}{p-1}<1 . The existence of self-similar blow up dyamics is known [51], and suitable self-similar blow up profiles were constructed in [2]. In this work, we establish the finite codimensional nonlinear asymptotic stability in homogeneous Sobolev space and energy space H^{1} for a large class of self-similar profiles. The heart of the proof is, following the approach of Beceanu [4], the derivation of Strichartz dispersive estimates for matrix operators of the form
\mathcal{H}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\Delta_{b}-1&\\
&-\Delta_{-b}+1\end{array}\right)-ibs_{c}+\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}W_{1}&W_{2}\\
-\overline{W_{2}}&-W_{1}\end{array}\right),
b>0 and
\Delta_{b}=\Delta+ib\left(\frac{d}{2}+x\cdot\nabla\right),
inhomogeneous Sobolev spaces. The deformed Laplacian \Delta_{b} arises from the renormalization and its operator group e^{it\Delta_{b}} exhibits self-similar dispersion, which not only recovers the free Strichartz but also enables an extension of resolvent families. Compared with Strichartz estimates based on \Delta , this one has a larger admissible region, works for arbitrarily small polynomial decaying potential, and requires no spectral assumption.
1. Introduction
1.1. Setting of the problem
We consider the nonlinear Schrödinger equation
\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+u|u|^{p-1}=0\\
u_{|t=0}=u_{0}\end{array}\right.
(NLS)
for spatial dimension d\geq 1 and p>1 . The scaling symmetry
u_{\lambda}(t,x):=\lambda^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(\lambda^{2}t,\lambda x),\quad\lambda>0
allows us to compute the critical Sobolev norm invariant
\|u_{\lambda}(t,\cdot)\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{c}}}=\|u(\lambda^{2}t,\cdot)\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{c}}},\quad s_{c}:=\frac{d}{2}-\frac{2}{p-1}.
In this paper, we are interested in describing singularity formation mechanisms for nonlinearities above the mass and below the energy conservation laws:
0<s_{c}<1.
1.2. Type I and Type II blowup.
We now recall some key facts related to the description of singularity formation for (NLS) with 0<s_{c}<1 .
The self-similar law. From an elementary scaling argument, all blow up solutions satisfy the scaling self-similar lower bound
\|u(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\gtrsim(T-t)^{-\frac{\sigma-s_{c}}{2}}
(1.1)
where s_{c}<\sigma\leq 1 is supercritical. We say a solution blows up self-similarily if it saturates the self-similar law
\|u(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\sim(T-t)^{-\frac{\sigma-s_{c}}{2}},\quad s_{c}<\sigma\leq 1.
(1.2)
Type II blow. Type II solutions which blow up strictly faster than (1.2) have been constructed both in the critical case s_{c}=0 , [53, 44, 46, 42, 43, 45, 54]), and the supercritical case through the derivation of "ring" solutions which concentrate on a circle, [22, 55, 52, 29].
Type I blow. However, for 0<s_{c}<1 , type I blow is conjectured to exist and generate stable blow up dynamics, [63, 62]. More precisely, the self-similar renormalization
u(t,x)=\frac{e^{i\gamma(t)}}{(\lambda(t))^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}v\left(\tau,y\right)
with the explicit laws
\lambda(t)=\sqrt{2b(T-t)},\quad\gamma(t)=\tau(t),\ \ \tau(t)=-\frac{1}{2b}\ln(T-t),\ \ y=\frac{x}{\lambda(t)}
(1.3)
maps (NLS) onto the renormalized flow
i\partial_{\tau}v+\Delta v-v+\frac{ib}{2}\left(\frac{2}{p-1}v+y\cdot\nabla v\right)+v|v|^{p-1}=0.
(1.4)
In the range 0<s_{c}<1 , admissible self-similar profiles are expected to exist from numerical grounds, [41, 36, 35, 62, 6, 5].
Conjecture (Existence of suitable profiles). Let d\geq 1 and s_{c}\in(0,1) . Then there exists b=b(d,s_{c})>0 and a smooth radially symmetric profile Q_{b} with the following properties.11

The equation (1.5) and self-similar decay (1.7) are essential, in that they can imply the non-vanishing property (1.6) and self-similar decay for higher order derivatives (1.8) via ODE analysis, see [66, Lemma 2.2] and [37] respectively. We remark that the main result of [66] was unfortunately dubious.
(i)
Equation: Q_{b} is a stationary solution to (1.4):
\Delta Q_{b}-Q_{b}+ib\left(\frac{2}{p-1}Q_{b}+y\cdot\nabla Q_{b}\right)+Q_{b}|Q_{b}|^{p-1}=0.
(1.5)
(ii)
Non-vanishing:
Q_{b}(x)\neq 0\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
(1.6)
(iii)
Self-similar decay:
\displaystyle\mathop{\rm lim}_{r\to\infty}r^{\frac{2}{p-1}}|Q_{b}(r)|=c_{p}>0,
\displaystyle\limsup_{r\to\infty}r^{\frac{p+1}{p-1}}|Q_{b}^{\prime}(r)|<\infty;
(1.7)
\displaystyle\limsup_{r\to\infty}r^{\frac{2}{p-1}+k}|\partial_{r}^{k}Q_{b}^{\prime}(r)|<\infty,
\displaystyle\forall\,\,k\geq 2.

The existence of such profiles has been obtained by Bahri-Martel-Raphaël [2] in the range 0<s_{c}\ll 1 by bifurcating from the critical case s_{c}=0 , see also [33] for the case of (gKdV). Extending the branch to higher values of s_{c} is a delicate nonlinear ODE problem, and recently Donninger-Shörkhuber [17] constructed the suitable profile for the physical scenario d=p=3 with computer assistance. Let us stress that the construction of self-similar profiles is central in the study of singularity formation mechanisms and has been mostly addressed in the energy supercritical case s_{c}>1 , see [12] for the heat equation, [13] for the wave equation and [28, 50] for compressible fluids.
Existence of self-similar dynamics. Self-similar profiles satisfying (1.7) are not in the energy space H^{1} and hence cannot be used as such to produce finite energy type I solutions. The existence of such dynamics was first obtained in [51] for 0<s_{c}\ll 1 using again a bifurcation argument from the critical case s_{c}=0 . The analysis provides solutions that satisfy the self-similar law (1.1), but does not describe the asymptotic structure of the singularity which should be given by the self-similar profile constructed in [2].
1.3. Main results
Our aim in this paper is to provide a robust approach for the proof of the asymptotic stability of self-similar profiles.
1.3.1. \dot{H}^{s_{c}+} stability theory
Theorem 1.1 (Finite-codimensional asymptotic stability in \dot{H}^{s_{c}+} ).

where \|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\ll 1 , such that the corresponding solution to (NLS) blows up at T=\frac{1}{2b} with a decomposition

6.3. Asymptotic stability in \dot{H}^{\sigma}
In this subsection, we will prove the nonlinear asymptotic stability in \dot{H}^{\sigma} by assuming mode stability Assumption 1.2 by a Brouwer argument for matching initial data.
We begin by computing the eigenpairs generated by symmetry.
Define
\xi_{0}=i\left(\begin{array}[]{c}Q_{b}\\
-{\overline{Q}}_{b}\end{array}\right),\,\,\xi_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\Lambda Q_{b}\\
\overline{\Lambda Q_{b}}\end{array}\right);\,\,\zeta_{j}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\partial_{j}Q_{b}\\
\overline{\partial_{j}Q_{b}}\end{array}\right),\,\,1\leq j\leq d.
(6.33)
where \Lambda=\frac{2}{p-1}+x\cdot\nabla .
Then \xi_{0},\xi_{1},\zeta_{j}\in X_{+} from their symmetry and the decay of Q_{b} (1.7).
By differentiating the self-similar profile equation (1.5) with respect to phase rotation, scaling and spatial translation, we obtain the algebraic relations
\displaystyle{\mathcal{H}}_{b}\xi_{0}=0,\quad{\mathcal{H}}_{b}\xi_{1}=-2bi\xi_{1}-i\xi_{0};\quad{\mathcal{H}}_{b}\zeta_{j}=-bi\zeta_{j},\quad 1\leq j\leq d.
Thus
{\mathcal{H}}_{b}\xi_{0}=0,\quad({\mathcal{H}}_{b}+2bi)\left(\xi_{0}+2b\xi_{1}\right)=0,\quad({\mathcal{H}}_{b}+bi)\zeta_{j}=0.
(6.34)
Proof of theorem 1.4.
Let \epsilon_{1}\leq\epsilon_{0} to be determined later, with \epsilon_{0} from Theorem 6.4. The explicit eigen relations (6.34) and mode stability Assumption 1.2 imply that
P_{u}X_{+}={\rm span}_{\mathbb{R}}(\xi_{0},\xi_{1},\zeta_{1},...,\zeta_{d}).
(6.35)
Step 1. Reduction to matching initial data.
Fix \varepsilon_{0}\in B^{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}_{\epsilon_{1}} . For \vec{\alpha}=(\lambda_{0},x_{0},\theta_{0}) , we define the modulated profile w_{0}^{\vec{\alpha}} to satisfy
(Q_{b}+\varepsilon_{0})(x)=\left(Q_{b}+w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}\right)\left(\frac{x-x_{0}}{\lambda_{0}}\right)\lambda_{0}^{-\frac{d}{2}+s_{c}}e^{-i\theta_{0}},
namely
w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}(y):=\left(Q_{b}+\varepsilon_{0}\right)\left(\lambda_{0}y+x_{0}\right)\lambda_{0}^{\frac{d}{2}-s_{c}}e^{i\theta_{0}}-Q_{b}(y).
(6.36)
We claim that for \epsilon_{1} small enough, there exists C_{*}>0 , such that there exists \vec{\alpha}\in B^{\mathbb{R}^{d+2}}_{C_{*}\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}} satisfying
\Phi\left((1-P_{u})\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}\right)=P_{u}\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}
(6.37)
where \Phi is the unstable-data map defined in Theorem 6.4.
Now we prove that (6.37) concludes the proof of Theorem 1.4.
Let
\tilde{u}_{0}:=Q_{b}+w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}=Q_{b}+\Pi(1-P_{u})\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}+\Pi\Phi\left((1-P_{u})\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}\right).
Since
\|\Pi(1-P_{u})\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\lesssim\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}+|\vec{\alpha}|\lesssim\epsilon_{1},
when \epsilon_{1} is small enough, we have \|\Pi(1-P_{u})\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\leq\epsilon_{0} and hence Theorem 6.4 implies that \tilde{u}_{0}
generates a self-similar blowup
\tilde{u}(t,x)=\frac{1}{(1-2bt)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}}(Q_{b}+w)\left(t,\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-2bt}}\right)e^{-i\frac{\ln(\frac{1}{2b}-t)}{2b}},\quad w\big|_{t=0}=w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0},
with w satisfies \|w(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}_{x}}\lesssim(1-2bt)^{\frac{\sigma-s_{c}}{2}} and there exists a blowup profile \tilde{u}_{*} in the sense of (6.18).
Then from the symmetry of (NLS), the solution generated by u_{0}=Q_{b}+\varepsilon_{0} becomes
u(t,x)=\tilde{u}\left(\frac{t}{\lambda_{0}^{2}},\frac{x-x_{0}}{\lambda_{0}}\right)\lambda_{0}^{-\frac{d}{2}+s_{c}}e^{-i\theta_{0}},
so (1.14) holds with \varepsilon(t)=w(\lambda_{0}^{-2}t) has desired decaying when t\to T:=\frac{\lambda_{0}^{2}}{2b} . The vanishing of \varepsilon(t) implies the uniqueness of the asymptotics decomposition (1.14), and hence the uniqueness of the modulation parameter \vec{\alpha} . The blowup profile for u is u_{*}=\tilde{u}_{*}\left(\frac{\cdot-x_{0}}{\lambda_{0}}\right)\lambda_{0}^{-\frac{d}{2}+s_{c}}e^{-i\theta_{0}} .
Step 2. Parameterization and Brouwer argument.
Now we prove the claim by solving (6.37).
Let
r_{\vec{\alpha}}:=Q_{b}(\lambda_{0}\cdot+x_{0})\lambda_{0}^{\frac{d}{2}-s_{c}}e^{i\theta_{0}}-Q_{b},\quad v_{\vec{\alpha}}=w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}-r_{\vec{\alpha}}=\varepsilon_{0}(\lambda_{0}\cdot+x_{0})\lambda_{0}^{\frac{d}{2}-s_{c}}e^{i\theta_{0}},
then (6.37) becomes
P_{u}\Pi^{-1}r_{\vec{\alpha}}=\Phi\left((1-P_{u})\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}\right)-P_{u}\Pi^{-1}v_{\vec{\alpha}}.
(6.38)
Since P_{u}\big|_{P_{u}X_{+}}=I\big|_{P_{u}X_{+}} , we compute
P_{u}\Pi^{-1}\left(\left(\partial_{\theta_{0}},\partial_{\lambda_{0}},\partial_{(x_{0})_{1}},...,\partial_{(x_{0})_{d}}\right)r_{\vec{\alpha}}\right)\Big|_{\vec{\alpha}=\vec{0}}=\left(\xi_{0},2\xi_{2},\zeta_{1},...,\zeta_{d}\right).

{\mathcal{P}}:P_{u}X_{+}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+2},\quad c_{1}\xi_{0}+2c_{2}\xi_{1}+\sum_{j=1}^{d}c_{j+2}\zeta_{j}\mapsto\vec{c},
which is clearly well-defined by the linear independence of those modes (6.33). Then {\mathcal{P}}P_{u}\Pi^{-1}(\nabla_{\vec{\alpha}}r_{\vec{\alpha}})\big|_{\vec{\alpha}=\vec{0}}={\rm Id}_{\mathbb{R}^{d+2}} and (6.38) turns into
\begin{split}\vec{\alpha}={\mathcal{T}}_{\varepsilon_{0}}(\vec{\alpha}):&=-{\mathcal{P}}P_{u}\Pi^{-1}\left(r_{\vec{\alpha}}-\vec{\alpha}\cdot(\nabla_{\vec{\alpha}}r_{\vec{\alpha}})\big|_{\vec{\alpha}=\vec{0}}\right)\\
&+{\mathcal{P}}\left[\Phi\left((1-P_{u})\Pi^{-1}w^{(\vec{\alpha})}_{0}\right)-P_{u}\Pi^{-1}v_{\vec{\alpha}}\right].\end{split}
(6.39)
From the boundedness of P_{u} , \Pi^{-1} , {\mathcal{P}} and (6.19), together with that for |\vec{\alpha}|\leq 1 ,
\left\|v_{\vec{\alpha}}\right\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\lesssim\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}},\quad\|r_{\vec{\alpha}}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\lesssim|\vec{\alpha}|,\quad\|r_{\vec{\alpha}}-\vec{\alpha}\cdot(\nabla_{\vec{\alpha}}r_{\vec{\alpha}})\big|_{\vec{\alpha}=\vec{0}}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\lesssim|\vec{\alpha}|^{2},
we have for |\vec{\alpha}|\leq 1 , there exists C_{*}>0 independent of \varepsilon_{0},\vec{\alpha} such that
\displaystyle\left|{\mathcal{T}}_{\varepsilon_{0}}(\vec{\alpha})\right|
\displaystyle\leq
\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}C_{*}\left(\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}+|\vec{\alpha}|^{\min\{p,2\}}\right).
Suppose
\epsilon_{1}<(2C_{*}^{\min\{p,2\}})^{\frac{1}{\min\{p-1,1\}}},
then with \|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}\leq\epsilon_{1} , we have
{\mathcal{T}}_{\varepsilon_{0}}\left(B^{\mathbb{R}^{d+2}}_{C_{*}\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}}\right)\subset B^{\mathbb{R}^{d+2}}_{C_{*}\|\varepsilon_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{\sigma}}},
and the Brouwer fixed point theorem implies the existence of solution \vec{\alpha} to (6.39) and hence (6.37). That concludes the proof.
∎

Moreover, the profiles satisfy repulsivity properties. That is, there exists \widetilde{\eta}>0 such that:

The properties (1.11)-(1.14) follow from the construction of the profiles easily, and we refer to [47, 7] for their justifications. The property (1.15) is essential for the radial stability and also proved in those papers. The property (1.16) is needed for the non-radial stability and requires substantial amount of work. Theorem 1.1.
Let \Psi_{p},S_{p} be self-similar profiles solving (1.10) for (d,p)=(8,3) and satisfying (1.11)–(1.14), for some r>2 . Let T>0 sufficiently small.
Then, there exists C^{\infty} initial data v_{0} for which equation (1.1) on \mathbb{T}^{d} blows up at time T in a self-similar manner. More concretely, for any fixed y\in\mathbb{T}^{d} , v(y,t)=\sqrt{\rho}(y,t)e^{i\Psi(y,t)} with \rho\in\mathbb{R}^{+} , \Psi\in\mathbb{R} , we have:
\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow T^{-}}r(T-t)^{1-\frac{2}{r}}\Psi\left((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}y,t\right)
\displaystyle=\Psi_{p}(|y|),
\displaystyle\lim_{t\rightarrow T^{-}}\left(\alpha^{-1}r(T-t)^{1-\frac{1}{r}}\right)^{1/\alpha}\rho\left((T-t)^{\frac{1}{r}}y,t\right)
\displaystyle=S_{p}(|y|)^{1/\alpha}\,.
Moreover, there exists a finite codimension set of initial data satisfying the above conclusions.
Theorem 1.2.
Let \Psi_{p},S_{p} be self-similar profiles solving (1.10) for (d,p)=(8,3) and satisfying (1.11)–(1.14), for some r>2 . Let T>0 sufficiently small.
Then, there exists C^{\infty} initial data v_{0} for which equation (1.1) on \mathbb{R}^{d} blows up at time T in a self-similar manner. More concretely, for any fixed y\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , v(y,t)=\sqrt{\rho}(y,t)e^{i\Psi(y,t)} with \rho\in\mathbb{R}^{+} , \Psi\in\mathbb{R} , we have:

Remark 1.3.
For simplicity, we have chosen to fix a particular instance of (d,p) . In principle, one could prove a similar result for other values of (d,p) using a similar study of the angular repulsivity property, and even a larger class by means of a computer-assisted proof as in [7].
Remark 1.4.
The Sobolev norm \|\nabla^{s}v\|_{L^{2}} blows up in both \mathbb{R}^{d} or \mathbb{T}^{d} when s>\frac{d}{2(r-1)}-\frac{2}{p-1}. In fact we have
\displaystyle\quad\|\nabla^{s}(\sqrt{\rho}e^{i\psi})\|_{L^{2}}^{2}

Remark 1.5.
In recent years several works have been put forward in which

the nature of the periodicity, namely the rationality or irrationality11

We say that a torus {\mathbb{T}}^{d} of periods T_{1},T_{2},\dots T_{d} is irrational if there is no non-zero vector \vec{w}=(w_{1},\dots,w_{d})\in\mathbb{Z}^{d} such that \sum_{i=1}^{d}w_{i}T_{i}=0 . of the domain {\mathbb{T}}^{d} , matters, see [33, 20, 22, 21, 57, 28, 30, 8, 35]. This physically makes sense since as time evolves the nonlinear solution starts seeing the different effects of the periodic boundary conditions. In our case, as one can gather from the conclusion of Theorem 1.1, we do not distinguish between a rational or irrational torus {\mathbb{T}}^{d} . This is because the blow up result we prove is localized and not close to the boundary. Of course we do not exclude that there could be other types of blow up mechanism that indeed are sensitive to the nature of the periodicity of the boundary, but the study of this phenomenon is not the scope of the present paper.

\displaystyle+(T-T_{0})^{\tilde{q}}e^{-\tilde{q}\tau}\sum_{k=3,4}\bigg(\Big\|\partial_{k}\tilde{B}\left(\tau,.,\textup{Re}(u_{1}+iu_{3}),\textup{Im}(u_{1}+iu_{3})\right) \displaystyle\times u_{l}(u_{1}^{\prime}+iu_{3}^{\prime}-(v_{1}^{\prime}+iv_{3}^{\prime}))\Big\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})} \displaystyle+\left\|\partial_{k}\tilde{B}\left(\tau,.,\textup{Re}(u_{1}+iu_{3}),\textup{Im}(u_{1}+iu_{3})\right)(v_{1}^{\prime}+iv_{3}^{\prime})(u_{l}-v_{l})\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\bigg) \displaystyle+(T-T_{0})e^{-\tau}\Big\|\tilde{B}\left(\tau,.,\textup{Re}(v_{1}+iv_{3}),\textup{Im}(v_{1}+iv_{3})\right)(u_{l}^{\prime}-v_{l}^{\prime})\Big\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})} \displaystyle+(T-T_{0})e^{-\tau}\Big\|u_{l}^{\prime}\big(\tilde{B}\left(\tau,.,\textup{Re}(u_{1}+iu_{3}),\textup{Im}(u_{1}+iu_{3})\right) \displaystyle-\tilde{B}\left(\tau,.,\textup{Re}(v_{1}+iv_{3}),\textup{Im}(v_{1}+iv_{3})\right)\big)\Big\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\bigg] \displaystyle\lesssim \displaystyle(T-T_{0})^{\tilde{q}}e^{-\tilde{q}\tau}\sum_{l=1}^{4}\Big(\|(1+|v_{1}+iv_{3}|)(u_{l}-v_{l})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}+\|u_{l}(u_{1}+iu_{3}-(v_{1}+iv_{3}))\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})} \displaystyle+\left\|u_{l}\left(u_{1}^{\prime}+iu^{\prime}_{3}-(v_{1}^{\prime}+iv_{3}^{\prime})\right)\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}+\left\|(v_{1}^{\prime}+iv_{3}^{\prime})\left(u_{l}-v_{l}\right)\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})} \displaystyle+\|(1+|v_{1}+iv_{3}|)(u_{l}^{\prime}-v_{l}^{\prime})\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}+\|u_{l}^{\prime}(u_{1}+iu_{3}-(v_{1}+iv_{3}))\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\Big) \displaystyle\lesssim \displaystyle(T-T_{0})^{\tilde{q}}e^{-\tilde{q}\tau}\bigg(\|\textup{{u}}-\textup{{v}}\|(1+\|\textup{{u}}\|+\|\textup{{v}}\|) \displaystyle+\sum_{l=1}^{4}\Big(\|u_{l}\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\|(u_{1}^{\prime}+iu^{\prime}_{3})-(v_{1}^{\prime}+iv_{3}^{\prime})\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})} \displaystyle+\|v_{1}^{\prime}+iv_{3}^{\prime}\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\|u_{l}-v_{l}\|_{L^{4}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}+\left(1+\|u_{1}+iu_{3}\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\right)\|u^{\prime}_{l}-v^{\prime}_{l}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})} \displaystyle+\|v_{l}^{\prime}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\|(u_{1}+iu_{3})-(v_{1}+iv_{3})\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{1})}\Big)\bigg) \displaystyle\lesssim \displaystyle(T-T_{0})^{\tilde{q}}e^{-\tilde{q}\tau}\|\textup{{u}}-\textup{{v}}\|\big(1+\|\textup{{u}}\|+\|\textup{{v}}\|\big), for \textup{{u}},\textup{{v}}\in\mathcal{H} and \tau\geq 0 . Since one can obtain the estimate \displaystyle I_{3}\lesssim(T-T_{0})^{\tilde{q}}e^{-\tilde{q}\tau}\|\textup{{u}}-\textup{{v}}\|\big(1+\|\textup{{u}}\|+\|\textup{{v}}\|\big) analogously, the proof of this Lemma is finished. ∎ These two Lemmas will be vital for the fixed point argument which will be done later on. We continue by employing Duhamel’s Principle, to rewrite Eq. (2.6) as an integral equation, which, for any initial data \Phi(0)=\textup{{u}}\in\mathcal{H} , takes the form \displaystyle\Phi(\tau)= \displaystyle\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau)\textup{{u}}+\int_{0}^{\tau}\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau-\sigma)\bigg(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma)) \displaystyle+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)}\bigg)\,d\sigma (3.2) for \tau\geq 0 and with the abbreviation \hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}=\textup{{L}}^{\prime}_{\theta(\sigma)}-\textup{{L}}^{\prime}_{\theta_{\infty}} . To analyse this equation further, we need the correct functional analytic setting and therefore introduce the two Banach spaces (\mathcal{X},\|.\|_{\mathcal{X}}) and (X,\|.\|_{X}) as follows. Definition 3.1.

4.1. The modulation equation
The instability corresponding to the eigenvalue 0 will be handled by modulation, i.e., by finding a function \theta(\tau) such that the instability is completely suppressed. To derive an equation for such a \theta , we formally apply the projection \textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}} to Eq. 3.2. This then yields
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\Phi(\tau)=
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}
\displaystyle+\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)d\sigma.
(4.1)
The idea now is to set the right-hand side equal to zero. But as this would entail the boundary condition \textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}=\textup{{0}} for \tau=0 , which is not always satisfied, we have to use a small trick. To this end, denote by \chi:[0,\infty)\to[0,1] a smooth cut-off function that satisfies \chi(\tau)=1 for \tau\in[0,1],\,\chi(\tau)=0 for \tau\geq 4 and finally |\chi^{\prime}(\tau)|\leq 1 for all \tau\geq 0 . Next, we make the ansatz \textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\Phi(\tau)=\chi(\tau)\tilde{\textup{{r}}} for some \tilde{\textup{{r}}}\in\textup{{rg}}\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}} .
Since evaluation at the time \tau=0 implies \tilde{\textup{{r}}}=\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}} , one obtains the modulation equation
\displaystyle\left(1-\chi(\tau)\right)
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}
\displaystyle+
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)\,d\sigma=0.
(4.2)
Now note that making the further assumption \theta(0)=0 yields
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\partial_{\sigma}\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)}\,d\sigma
\displaystyle=\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\dot{\theta}(\sigma)\left(\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}+\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)\,d\sigma
\displaystyle=\left(\theta(\tau)\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}+\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\dot{\theta}(\sigma)\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}d\sigma\right).
If we insert this into Eq. (4.2), we obtain
\displaystyle\theta(\tau)\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}=\left(1-\chi(\tau)\right)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}+
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\left(\Phi(\sigma)\right)+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)\,d\sigma
(4.3)
\displaystyle-
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}\dot{\theta}(\sigma)\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\,d\sigma.
The next Lemma will show that, provided \Phi is sufficiently small in norm, there is indeed a \theta:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that Eq. (4.3) is satisfied.
Lemma 4.1.
Suppose \delta>0 is sufficiently small and c>1 is sufficiently large. Furthermore let \Phi\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} and \textup{{u}}\in\mathcal{H} with \|\textup{{u}}\|\leq\frac{\delta}{c} . Then there exists a unique function \theta\in X_{\delta} such that \theta satisfies Eq. (4.3) and such that the map
\Phi\mapsto\theta:\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\subset\mathcal{X}\rightarrow X is Lipschitz-continuous.
Proof.
The idea to prove this, is by setting up a contraction for \theta . To this end, we begin by rewriting Eq. (4.3) as
\displaystyle\theta(\tau)\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}=
\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\tau}\chi^{\prime}(\sigma)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}\,d\sigma
\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{\tau}\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma))+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)\right)\,d\sigma
\displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\tau}\dot{\theta}(\sigma)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\,d\sigma
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle:\int_{0}^{\tau}\textup{{G}}(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\sigma)\,d\sigma.
This yields
\theta(\tau)\|\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\|^{2}=\left(\int_{0}^{\tau}\textup{{G}}(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\sigma)\,d\sigma\Big|\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\right).
Therefore, by setting
\tilde{G}(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\sigma)=\|\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\|^{-2}\left(\textup{{G}}(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\sigma)\big|\textup{{r}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\right),
we obtain
\theta(\tau)=\int_{0}^{\tau}\tilde{G}(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\sigma)\,d\sigma=:G(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\tau).
Thanks to Lemma 2.11, we know that
\|\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta(\tau)}\|\lesssim|\theta(\tau)-\theta_{\infty}|\lesssim\delta e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}.
Further, it is also clear that
\|\chi^{\prime}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}\|\lesssim\|\chi^{\prime}(\tau)\textup{{u}}\|\lesssim\frac{\delta}{c}e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}.
Thus Lemma 3.3 implies \|\textup{{G}}(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|\lesssim(\frac{\delta}{c}+\delta^{2})e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau} , from which we conclude that for \theta\in X_{\delta} we have
G(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})\in X_{\delta}
provided that \delta>0 and c>0 are chosen sufficiently small and large, respectively.
Next, note that
\|\chi^{\prime}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{u}}-\chi^{\prime}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{u}}\|\lesssim\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}|\theta_{1_{\infty}}-\theta_{2_{\infty}}|\lesssim\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X}
as well as
\displaystyle\|\dot{\theta}_{1}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{1}(\tau)}-\dot{\theta}_{2}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{2}(\tau)}\|\leq
\displaystyle\|\dot{\theta}_{1}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{1}(\tau)}-\dot{\theta}_{1}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{2}(\tau)}\|
\displaystyle+
\displaystyle\|\dot{\theta}_{1}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{2}(\tau)}-\dot{\theta}_{2}(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{2}(\tau)}\|
\displaystyle\lesssim
\displaystyle\delta e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}\|\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{1}(\tau)}-\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{2}(\tau)}\|+\delta e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}|\dot{\theta}_{1}-\dot{\theta}_{2}|
\displaystyle\lesssim
\displaystyle\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X},
since \|\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}-\hat{\textup{{r}}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\|\lesssim e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X}.
These two estimates together with the estimates provided by Lemma 3.4 now imply that
\|\textup{{G}}(\theta_{1},\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{G}}(\theta_{2},\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|\lesssim\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X}
which in turn yields
\|G(\theta_{1},\Phi,\textup{{u}})-G(\theta_{2},\Phi,\textup{{u}})\|_{X}\lesssim\delta\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X},
(4.4)
for all \theta_{1},\theta_{2}\in X_{\delta} . Therefore, the requirements of the contraction mapping principle are satisfied and we obtain the existence of a unique \theta\in X_{\delta} with \theta(\tau)=G(\theta,\Phi,\textup{{u}})(\tau) . To prove the final claim, let \theta_{1}(\tau)=G(\theta_{1},\Phi_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau) and \theta_{2}(\tau)=G(\theta_{2},\Phi_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau),
for \Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}. We then estimate
\displaystyle|\dot{\theta}_{1}(\tau)-\dot{\theta}_{2}(\tau)|\lesssim
\displaystyle|\,G(\theta_{1},\Phi_{1},\textup{{u}})-G(\theta_{2},\Phi_{2},\textup{{u}})\,|
\displaystyle\lesssim
\displaystyle\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\left(\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}+\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X}\right),
due to the previous considerations in this proof and the estimates in Lemma 3.4.
This now yields the claim by invoking the fundamental theorem of calculus, provided \delta is chosen sufficiently small.
∎
4.2. Time-translation instability
Now we deal with the unstable subspace \textup{{rg}}\,\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}. This will be done by adding a correction term to the evolution in order to stabilize it. To find such a term, we formally apply \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}} to Eq. (4.2) which yields
\displaystyle\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\Phi(\tau)=
\displaystyle\,e^{\tau}\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}
\displaystyle+e^{\tau}\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-\sigma}\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma))+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)\,d\sigma
\displaystyle-e^{\tau}\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-\sigma}\partial_{\sigma}\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)}\,d\sigma.
Therefore, we set
\displaystyle\textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}):=\,
\displaystyle\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}}
\displaystyle+
\displaystyle\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\sigma}\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma))+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Phi_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)\,d\sigma
and first deal with the modified equation given by
\displaystyle\Phi(\tau)=
\displaystyle\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau)\left(\textup{{u}}-\textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\right)
\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{\tau}\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau-\sigma)\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma))+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Phi_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)\,d\sigma.
(4.5)
Proposition 4.1.
Let \delta>0 be small enough and c\geq 1 be sufficiently large. For any \textup{{u}}\in\mathcal{H} with \|\textup{{u}}\|\leq\frac{\delta}{c} there exist unique functions \Phi\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} and \theta\in X_{\delta} such that equation (4.5) holds for all \tau\geq 0 .
Proof.
To begin with, we denote the right-hand side of Eq. (4.5) by \textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau). The idea of this proof is to again invoke the contraction mapping principle. Therefore, we first claim that for \delta>0 small enough and \Phi\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} we have \textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} where \theta\in X_{\delta} is the one associated to \Phi by Lemma 4.1.
We first apply the projection \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}} to the right-hand side of the equation which yields
\displaystyle\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau)=
\displaystyle-\int_{\tau}^{\infty}e^{\tau-\sigma}\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\bigg(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma)
\displaystyle+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Phi_{\theta(\sigma)}\bigg)\,d\sigma.
Therefore, Lemma 3.3 implies
\displaystyle\|\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|\lesssim\delta^{2}\int_{\tau}^{\infty}e^{\tau-\sigma}e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\lesssim\delta^{2}e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}.
Thus \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\in\mathcal{X}_{\frac{\delta}{4}} if \delta is chosen small enough. Note that since \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}=0 and \textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) is contained in the range of \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}} , we obtain
\displaystyle\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau)=\chi(\tau)\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{u}},
due to Eq. (4.2).
Hence
\displaystyle\|\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|\lesssim\frac{\delta}{c}e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}
and, provided c is chosen sufficiently large, this implies
\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\in\mathcal{X}_{\frac{\delta}{4}} .
To show that \textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} , it remains to consider \left(\textup{{I}}-\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\right)\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau), which equals
\displaystyle\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau)\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\left(\textup{{u}}+\textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\right)
\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{\tau}
\displaystyle\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau-\sigma)\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma))+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Phi_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)\,d\sigma
with \tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta_{\infty}} defined as in Proposition 2.2.
Thanks to Lemma 3.4, we have
\|\textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\|\lesssim\frac{\delta}{c}+\delta^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\sigma-2\omega_{p}\sigma}\,d\sigma\lesssim\frac{\delta}{c}+\delta^{2}
and therefore, from Proposition 2.2 and Lemma 3.3, we infer
\displaystyle\|\left(\textup{{I}}-\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\right)\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|
\displaystyle\lesssim(\frac{\delta}{c}+\delta^{2})e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}+\delta^{2}\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-\omega_{p}(\tau-\sigma)}e^{-2\omega_{p}\sigma}\,d\sigma
\displaystyle\lesssim(\frac{\delta}{c}+\delta^{2})e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}.
In summary, \textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}})\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} whenever \Phi\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} .
It remains to show the Lipschitz-continuity of \textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) for arbitrary \Phi\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} .
Hence let \Phi_{1},\Phi_{2}\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta} and let \theta_{i} be associated to \Phi_{i} through Lemma 4.1. We proceed in a similar manner as before and therefore first deal with \textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) . This yields
\displaystyle\|
\displaystyle\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|
\displaystyle\lesssim
\displaystyle\|\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau\textbf{})\|
\displaystyle+\|\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{Q}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|
\displaystyle\lesssim
\displaystyle\delta\int_{\tau}^{\infty}e^{\tau-\sigma}e^{-2\omega_{p}\sigma}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}d\sigma
\displaystyle\lesssim
\displaystyle\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}},
by using the estimates given in Lemma 3.4 as well as the estimate
\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X}\lesssim\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}
which was derived in Lemma 4.1.
We further obtain
\displaystyle\|\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|
\displaystyle\lesssim|\chi(\tau)|\,\|(\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}-\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}})\textup{{u}}\|
\displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}\|_{X}
\displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-2\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}},
due to the Lemmas 2.11 and 4.1.
By invoking Lemmas 2.11 and 3.4, one obtains
\displaystyle\|\textup{{C}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})-\textup{{C}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})\|
\displaystyle\lesssim\delta\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}+\delta\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\sigma-2\omega_{p}\sigma}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}
\displaystyle\lesssim\delta\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}.
Hence,
\displaystyle\|\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta_{1_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{1},\theta_{1},\textup{{u}})(\tau)-\tilde{\textup{{P}}}_{\theta_{2_{\infty}}}\textup{{K}}(\Phi_{2},\theta_{2},\textup{{u}})(\tau)\|
\displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}
\displaystyle+\delta\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-\omega_{p}(\tau+\sigma)}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}
\displaystyle\lesssim\delta e^{-\omega_{p}\tau}\|\Phi_{1}-\Phi_{2}\|_{\mathcal{X}}
again with the help of the Lemmas 2.11 and 3.4.
The claim is now established, since the conditions of the aforementioned contraction mapping principle have been established.
∎

4.3. Variation of blowup time
We are now going to develop tools that allow us to solve Eq. (4.5) without the correction term \textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{u}}) . In order to do so, we first introduce the scaling operator \textup{{v}}\mapsto\textup{{v}}^{T} with
\displaystyle\textup{{v}}^{T}(\rho):=\begin{pmatrix}&(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}v_{1}((T-T_{0})\rho)\\
&(T-T_{0})^{\frac{p+1}{p-1}}v_{2}((T-T_{0})\rho)\\
&(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}v_{3}((T-T_{0})\rho)\\
&(T-T_{0})^{\frac{p+1}{p-1}}v_{4}((T-T_{0})\rho)\end{pmatrix}
for any \textup{{v}}\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R}):=\{\textup{{v}}\in(H^{2}\times H^{1}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R}))^{2}:\textup{{v}}\text{ radial}\} .
We do this since, due to transformations we applied to Eq. (1.1), the blowup time is now also showing up in the initial data of Eq. (1.11). By the splitting 1.12, the initial data can the be rewritten as
\displaystyle\Phi(0)=\Psi(0)-\Psi_{\theta(0)}(0)=\textup{{J}}(\tilde{f},\tilde{g})^{T}+\Psi_{0}^{T}-\Psi_{0}
where \textup{{J}}:H^{2}\times H^{1}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R}) with
\textup{{J}}(\tilde{f},\tilde{g})(\rho):=\begin{pmatrix}&\textup{Re}\left(\tilde{f}(\rho)\right)\\
&\textup{Re}\left(\tilde{g}(\rho)\right)\\
&\textup{Im}\left(\tilde{f}(\rho)\right)\\
&\textup{Im}\left(\tilde{g}(\rho)\right)\end{pmatrix}
Note that J is a bounded linear operator. Motivated by this, we set
\displaystyle\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}):=\textup{{J}}(\textup{{v}})^{T}+\Psi_{0}^{T}-\Psi_{0}
for any \textup{{v}}\in H^{2}\times H^{1}(\mathbb{B}^{3}_{R}). Further, by setting \textup{{v}}:=(\tilde{f},\tilde{g}) we can rewrite our initial data as
\Phi(0)=\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}).
Next, we need the following result on U.
Lemma 4.2.
Let \delta>0 be small enough, c\geq 1 sufficiently large, T_{0}\in[1-\frac{3\delta}{c},1-\frac{2\delta}{c}] and T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] . Furthermore, suppose \|\textup{{v}}\|_{H^{2}\times H^{1}(\mathbb{B}_{R}^{3})} is sufficiently small, where R=\frac{3\delta}{c}+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}. Then
\|\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})\|\leq\delta,
for all T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] and the map
T\mapsto\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}):[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}]\rightarrow\mathcal{H} is continuous.
Proof.
First note that
\displaystyle\left|[\Psi_{0}^{T}]_{1}-[\Psi_{0}]_{1}\right|
\displaystyle=\kappa_{p}\left|\frac{(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}{(1-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}}}-1\right|
\displaystyle\lesssim\left|\frac{T-T_{0}-1+T_{0}}{1-T_{0}}\right|^{\frac{2}{p-1}}
\displaystyle\leq\left|\frac{1-T}{1-T_{0}}\right|^{\frac{2}{p-1}}
\displaystyle\lesssim\left|c\right|^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}.
Further, the same estimate holds true for the other components as well.
To continue let \textup{{v}}\in\mathcal{H}(\mathbb{B}_{R}^{3}) . Then
\displaystyle\|\textup{{v}}^{T}\|\lesssim
\displaystyle(T-T_{0})^{\frac{2}{p-1}-3}\|\textup{{v}}\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{B}_{T-T_{0}}^{3})}
\displaystyle\lesssim
\displaystyle\left(\frac{c}{\delta}\right)^{3-\frac{2}{p-1}}\|\textup{{v}}\|_{H^{2}(\mathbb{B}_{R}^{3})}.
Therefore, as \|\textup{{J}}\|=1 , we obtain \|\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})\|\leq\delta , provided v satisfies

and c is chosen large enough.
∎
This result immediately implies the following Lemma.
Lemma 4.3.
Assume that the assumptions of Lemma 4.2 hold. Then the equation
\displaystyle\Phi(\tau)=
\displaystyle\,\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau)\left(\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})-\textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}))\right)
(4.6)
\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{\tau}\textup{{S}}_{\theta_{\infty}}(\tau-\sigma)\left(\hat{\textup{{L}}}_{\theta(\sigma)}\Phi(\sigma)+\textup{{N}}_{\theta(\sigma)}(\Phi(\sigma))+\textup{{V}}(\Phi(\sigma)+\Psi_{\theta(\sigma)},\sigma)-\partial_{\sigma}\Phi_{\theta(\sigma)}\right)\,d\sigma
has a solution (\Phi,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\times X_{\delta} and the solution map T\mapsto(\Phi,\theta):[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}]\rightarrow\mathcal{X}\times X is continuous.
Proof.
This follows immediately from Lemma 4.2, since one obtains Eq. (4.6) by replacing u with \textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}) in Eq. (4.5).
∎
The final Lemma, needed to prove the main result, states that we can choose a T such that the correction term \textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})) vanishes.
Lemma 4.4.
Let the assumptions be as in Lemma 4.2. Then, there exist functions (\Phi,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\times X_{\delta} and a T\in[1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] such that Eq. (4.6) holds with \textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}))=\textup{{0}} .
Proof.
Denote by (\Phi,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}_{\delta}\times X_{\delta} , the functions associated to T through Lemma 4.3.
Further note that
\partial_{T}\Psi_{0}^{T}|_{T=1}=C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\textup{{g}}_{0}(\rho),
for some constant C_{p}>0 .
Therefore we can rewrite \textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}) as
\displaystyle\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})=
\displaystyle J(\textup{{v}})^{T}+(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\textup{{g}}_{0}+(T-1)^{2}(T-T_{0})^{2}\textup{{f}}(T)
\displaystyle=
\displaystyle J(\textup{{v}})^{T}+(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}+(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}(\textup{{g}}_{\theta(0)}-\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}})
\displaystyle+(T-1)^{2}(T-T_{0})^{2}\textup{{f}}(T)
with \|\textup{{f}}\|\lesssim 1.
As |\theta(0)-\theta_{\infty}|\lesssim\delta , we have that
\|\textup{{g}}_{\theta(0)}-\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\|\lesssim\delta
and from this we infer that
\displaystyle\left(\textup{{P}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}})|\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\right)=(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\|\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\|^{2}+O(\frac{\delta}{c})+O(c^{-2}),
where each of the O -terms is a continuous function of T .
Hence Lemma 4.3 implies that
\displaystyle\left(\textup{{C}}(\Phi,\theta,\textup{{U}}(T,\textup{{v}}))|\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\right)=(T-1)C_{p}(T-T_{0})^{-1}\|\textup{{g}}_{\theta_{\infty}}\|^{2}+O(\frac{\delta}{c})+O(c^{-2}).

\displaystyle 1-T=(T-T_{0})\left(O(\frac{\delta}{c})+O(c^{-2})\right).
Note that the right hand side, denoted by F(T) , is continuous in T and satisfies
|F|\leq\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}.
It follows that 1+F is a continuous map from [1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}] to [1-\frac{\delta}{c^{2}},1+\frac{\delta}{c^{2}}]
and such a map necessarily has a fixed point.
∎
Now we are able to prove our main result.

LAGA, CNRS (UMR 7539), F-93430, Villetaneuse, France. Note: This author is supported by the ERC Advanced Grant no. 291214, BLOWDISOL and by the ANR project ANAÉ ref. ANR-13-BS01-0010-03. Abstract We construct a solution for a class of strongly perturbed semilinear heat equations which blows up in finite time with a prescribed blow-up profile. The construction relies on the reduction of the problem to a finite dimensional one and the use of index theory to conclude. Keywords: Blow-up profile, finite-time blow-up, stability, semilinear heat equations. 1 Introduction We are interested in the following nonlinear parabolic equation: \left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}&=&\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u+h(u),\\ u(0)&=&u_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\end{array}\right. (1) where u is defined for (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T) , 1

1,\;M>0, (2) or h(z)=\mu\dfrac{|z|^{p-1}z}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}\;\;\;\text{with}\;\;a>0,\;\mu\in\mathbb{R}. (3) By standard results, the Cauchy problem for equation (1) can be solved in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) . The solution u(t) of (1) would exist either on [0,+\infty) (global existence) or only on [0,T) , with 01 , where f(z)=\kappa\left(1+c_{p}|z|^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad\text{with}\;\;c_{p}=\frac{p-1}{4p}. (8) The goal of this work is to show that the behavior (7) does occur. More precisely, we construct a blow-up solution of equation (1) satisfying the behavior described in (7). This is our main result: Theorem 1 (Existence of a blow-up solution for equation (1) with the description of its profile). There exists T>0 such that equation (1) has a solution u(x,t) in \mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T) satisfying: i) the solution u blows up in finite-time T at the point b=0 , ii) \left\|(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(\cdot\sqrt{T-t},t)-f\left(\frac{\cdot}{\sqrt{|\log(T-t)|}}\right)\right\|_{W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq\frac{C}{|\log(T-t)|^{\varrho}}, (9) for all \varrho\in(0,\nu) with \nu=\min\{a-1,\frac{1}{2}\} in the case (2) and \nu=\min\{a,\frac{1}{2}\} in the case (3), C is some positive constant and f is defined in (8). iii) There exists u_{*}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\},\mathbb{R}) such that u(x,t)\to u_{*}(x) as t\to T uniformly on compact subsets of \mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\} , where u_{*}(x)\sim\left(\frac{8p|\log|x||}{(p-1)^{2}|x|^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}\quad\text{as}\quad x\to 0. Remark 1. Note that i) directly follows from ii) . Indeed, ii) implies that u(0,t)\sim\kappa(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\to+\infty as t\to T , which means that u blows up in finite-time T at the point 0 . From iii) , we see that u blows up only at the point b=0 . Remark 2. Note that the profile f is the same as in the nonlinear heat equation without the perturbation ( h\equiv 0 ), see Bricmont and Kupiainen [3], Merle and Zaag [16]. The estimate (9) holds in W^{1,\infty} and uniformly in z\in\mathbb{R}^{n} . In the previous work, Ebde and Zaag [4] gives such a uniform convergence in the case h involving a nonlinear gradient term. In fact, the convergence in W^{1,\infty} comes from a parabolic regularity estimate for equation (5) (see Proposition 5 below). Dealing with the case h\equiv 0 , Bricmont and Kupiainen [3], Merle and Zaag [16] also give such a uniform convergence but only in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) . In most papers, the same kind convergence is proved, but only uniformly on a smaller subsets, |z|\leq K\sqrt{|\log(T-t)|} (see Velázquez [23]). The proof of Theorem 1 bases on techniques developed by Bricmont and Kupiainen in [3] and Merle and Zaag in [16] for the semilinear heat equation u_{t}=\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u. (10) Note that the perturbation term h certainly impacts on the construction of solutions of (1) satisfying (9). This causes some crucial modifications in [16] in order to totally control the term h . Although these modifications do not affect the general framework developed in [16], they lay in 3 crucial places: - We modify the profile around which we study equation (5), so that we go beyond the order \frac{1}{s^{a}} generated by the perturbation term. Indeed, for small a>0 and with the same profile as in [16], the order \frac{1}{s^{a}} will become too strong and will not allow us to close our estimates. See Section 2 below, particularly definition (12), which enables us to reach the order \frac{1}{s^{a+1}} . - In order to handle the order \frac{1}{s^{a+1}} , we need to modify the definition of the shrinking set near the profile. See Section 3 and particularly Proposition 3 below. - A sharp understanding of the dynamics of the linearized operator of (5) around the profile (12), and which allows to handle the new definition of the shrinking set. See Lemma (7) below. For that reason, we will stress only the main parts of the proof of Theorem 1 and put forward the novelties of our argument. In particular, the proof relies on the understanding of the dynamics of the self-similar version of equation (5) around the profile (8). Following the work by Merle and Zaag [16], the proof will be divided into 2 steps: - In the first step, we reduce the problem to a finite-dimensional problem: we will show that it is enough to control a finite-dimensional variable in order to control the solution near the profile. - In the second step, we proceed by contradiction to solve the finite-dimensional problem and conclude using index theory. We would like to mention that Masmoudi and Zaag [14] adapted the method of [16] for the following Ginzburg-Landau equation: u_{t}=(1+\imath\beta)\Delta u+(1+\imath\delta)|u|^{p-1}u, (11) where p-\delta^{2}-\beta\delta(p+1)>0 and u:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T)\to\mathbb{C} . Note that the case \beta=0 and \delta\in\mathbb{R} small has been studied earlier by Zaag [26]. In [22], Nouaili and Zaag successfully used the method of [16] for the following complex valued semilinear heat equation: u_{t}=\Delta u+u^{2}, where u(t):x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{C} . As in [16], [26] and [14], it is possible to make the interpretation of the finite-dimensional variable in terms of the blow-up time and the blow-up point. This allows us to derive the stability of the profile f in Theorem 1 with respect to perturbations in the initial data. More precisely, we have the following: Theorem 2 (Stability of the solution constructed in Theorem 1). Let us denote by \hat{u}(x,t) the solution constructed in Theorem 1 and by \hat{T} its blow-up time. Then, there exists a neighborhood \mathcal{V}_{0} of \hat{u}(x,0) in W^{1,\infty} such that for any u_{0}\in\mathcal{V}_{0} , equation (1) has a unique solution u(x,t) with initial data u_{0} , and u(x,t) blows up in finite time T(u_{0}) at one single blow-up point b(u_{0}) . Moreover, estimate (7) is satisfied by u(x-b,t) and T(u_{0})\to\hat{T},\quad b(u_{0})\to 0\quad\text{as $u_{0}\to\hat{u}_{0}$ in $W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})$}. Remark 3. We will not give the proof of Theorem 2 because the stability result follows from the reduction to a finite dimensional case as in [16] with the same proof. Hence, we only prove the reduction and refer to [16] for the stability. Note that from the parabolic regularity, our stability result holds in the larger space L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) . 2 Formulation of the problem As in [16], [3], we give the proof in one dimension ( n=1 ). The proof remains the same for higher dimensions ( n\geq 2 ). We would like to find u_{0} initial data such that the solution u of equation (1) blows up in finite time T and satisfies the estimate (9). Using similarity variables (4), this is equivalent to finding s_{0}>0 and w_{0}(y)\equiv w(y,s_{0}) such that the solution w of equation (5) with initial data w_{0} satisfies \lim_{s\to+\infty}\|w(y,s)-f(\frac{y}{\sqrt{s}})\|_{W^{1,\infty}}=0, where f is given in (8). In order to prove this, we will not linearize equation (5) around f+\frac{\kappa}{2ps} as in [16]. We will instead introduce q=w-\varphi,\quad\text{where}\quad\varphi=\frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa}\left(f(\frac{y}{\sqrt{s}})+\frac{\kappa}{2ps}\right), (12) with \phi and f are introduced in (6) and (8). Then, the problem is reduced to constructing a function q such that \lim_{s\to+\infty}\|q(y,s)\|_{W^{1,\infty}}=0 and q is a solution of the following equation for all (y,s)\in\mathbb{R}\times[s_{0},+\infty) , q_{s}=(\mathcal{L}+V)q+B(q)+R(y,s)+N(y,s), (13) where \mathcal{L}=\Delta-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla+1 and \displaystyle V(y,s) \displaystyle=p\left(\varphi(y,s)^{p-1}-\frac{1}{p-1}\right)+\imath e^{-s}h^{\prime}(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi), (14) \displaystyle B(q) \displaystyle=|\varphi+q|^{p-1}(\varphi+q)-\varphi^{p}-p\varphi^{p-1}q, (15) \displaystyle R(y,s) \displaystyle=-\varphi_{s}+\Delta\varphi-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla\varphi-\frac{\varphi}{p-1}+\varphi^{p}+e^{\frac{-ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi\right), (16) \displaystyle N(q,s) \displaystyle=e^{\frac{-ps}{p-1}}\left[h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}(\varphi+q)\right)-h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi\right)-\imath e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\varphi\right)q\right], (17) with \imath=0 in the case (2) and \imath=1 in the case (3). One can remark that we don’t linearize (5) around \tilde{\varphi}=f(\frac{y}{\sqrt{s}})+\frac{\kappa}{2ps} as in the case of equation (10) treated in [16]. In fact, if we do the same, we may obtain some terms like \frac{1}{s^{a}} coming from the strong perturbation h in equation (5), and we may not be able to control these terms in the case a<3 . To extend the range of a , we multiply the factor \frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa} to \tilde{\varphi} in order to go beyond the order \frac{1}{s^{a}} and reach at the order \frac{1}{s^{a+1}} . Linearizing around \varphi given in (12) is a major novelty in our approach. In following analysis, we will use the following integral form of equation (13): for each s\geq\sigma\geq s_{0} : q(s)=\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma)q(\sigma)+\int_{\sigma}^{s}\mathcal{K}(s,\tau)\left[B(q(\tau))+R(\tau)+N(q(\tau),\tau)\right]d\tau, (18) where \mathcal{K} is the fundamental solution of the linear operator \mathcal{L}+V defined for each \sigma>0 and for each s\geq\sigma , \partial_{s}\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma)=(\mathcal{L}+V)\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma),\quad\mathcal{K}(\sigma,\sigma)=Identity. (19) Since the dynamics of equation (13) are influenced by the linear part, we first need to recall some properties of the operator \mathcal{L} from Bricmont and Kupiainen [3]. The operator \mathcal{L} is self-adjoint in L^{2}_{\rho}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) , where L^{2}_{\rho} is the weighted L^{2} space associated with the weight \rho defined by \rho(y)=\left(\frac{1}{4\pi}\right)^{n/2}e^{-\frac{|y|^{2}}{4}}. Its spectrum is given by spec(\mathcal{L})=\{1-\frac{m}{2},\;m\in\mathbb{N}\}, and its eigenfunctions are derived from Hermite polynomials. If n=1 , the eigenfunction corresponding to 1-\frac{m}{2} is h_{m}(y)=\sum_{k=0}^{\left[\frac{m}{2}\right]}\frac{m!}{k!(m-2k)!}(-1)^{k}y^{m-2k}. (20) We also denote k_{m}(y)=\frac{h_{m}(y)}{\|h_{m}(y)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}^{2}} . If n\geq 2 , we write the spectrum of \mathcal{L} as spec(\mathcal{L})=\{1-\frac{|m|}{2},\;|m|=m_{1}+\dots+m_{n},\;(m_{1},\dots,m_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n}\} . Given m=(m_{1},\dots,m_{n})\in\mathbb{N}^{n} , the eigenfunction corresponding to 1-\frac{|m|}{2} is H_{m}(y)=h_{m_{1}}(y_{1})\dots h_{m_{n}}(y_{n}),\quad\text{where $h_{m}$ is defined in \eqref{equ:eigenfu1}.} (21) The potential V(y,s) has two fundamental properties: i) V(\cdot,s)\to 0 in L^{2}_{\rho} as s\to+\infty . In particular, the effect of V on the bounded sets or in the "blow-up" region ( |y|\leq K\sqrt{s} ) is regarded as a perturbation of the effect of \mathcal{L} . ii) outside of the "blow-up" region, we have the following property: for all \epsilon>0 , there exist C_{\epsilon}>0 and s_{\epsilon} such that \sup_{s\geq s_{\epsilon},|y|\geq C_{\epsilon}\sqrt{s}}|V(y,s)-(-\frac{p}{p-1})|\leq\epsilon. (22) This means that \mathcal{L}+V behaves like \mathcal{L}-\frac{p}{p-1} in the region |y|\geq K\sqrt{s} . Because 1 is the biggest eigenvalue of \mathcal{L} , the operator \mathcal{L}-\frac{p}{p-1} has purely negative spectrum. Therefore, the control of q(y,s) in L^{\infty} outside of the "blow-up" region will be done without difficulties. Since the behavior of V inside and outside of the "blow-up" region are different, let us decompose q as following: Let \chi_{0}\in\mathcal{C}_{0}^{\infty}([0,+\infty)) with supp(\chi_{0})\subset[0,2] and \chi_{0}\equiv 1 on [0,1] . We define \chi(y,s)=\chi_{0}(\frac{|y|}{K\sqrt{s}}), (23) where K>0 to be fixed large enough, and write q(y,s)=q_{b}(y,s)+q_{e}(y,s), (24) where q_{b}(y,s)=\chi(y,s)q(y,s) and q_{e}(y,s)=(1-\chi(y,s))q(y,s) . Note that supp(q_{b}(s))\subset\mathbf{B}(0,2K\sqrt{s}) and supp(q_{e}(s))\subset\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbf{B}(0,K\sqrt{s}) . In order to control q_{b} , we expand it with respect to the spectrum of \mathcal{L} in L^{2}_{\rho} . More precisely, we write q into 5 components as follows: q(y,s)=\sum_{m=0}^{2}q_{m}(s)h_{m}(y)+q_{-}(y,s)+q_{e}(y,s), (25) where q_{m},q_{-} are coordinates of q_{b} (not of q ), namely that q_{m} is the projection of q_{b} in h_{m} and q_{-}=P_{-}(q_{b}) with P_{-} being the projector on the negative subspace of \mathcal{L} . 3 Proof of the existence of a blow-up solution with the given blow-up profile In this section, we use the framework developed in [16] in order to prove Theorem 1. We proceed in 4 steps: - In the first step, we define a shrinking set V_{A}(s) and translate our goal of making q(s) go to 0 in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) in terms of belonging to V_{A}(s) . We also exhibit a two parameter initial data family for equation (13) whose coordinates are very small (with respect to the requirements of V_{A}(s) ), except the two first q_{0} and q_{1} . Note that the set V_{A}(s) is different from the corresponding one in [16], and this makes the second major novelty of our work, in addition to the modification of the profile in (12). - In the second step, using the spectral properties of equation (13), we reduce our goal from the control of q(s) (an infinite dimensional variable) in V_{A}(s) to the control of its two first components (q_{0}(s),q_{1}(s)) (a two-dimensional variable) in \left[-\frac{A}{s^{1+\nu}},\frac{A}{s^{1+\nu}}\right]^{2} with \nu>0 . - In the third step, we solve the local in time Cauchy problem for equation (13). - In the last step, we solve the finite dimensional problem using index theory and conclude the proof of Theorem 1. In what follows, the constant C denotes a universal one independent of variables, only depending upon constants of the problems such as a , p , M , \mu and K in (23). 3.1 Definition of a shrinking set V_{A}(s) and preparation of initial data Let first introduce the following proposition: Proposition 3 (A shrinking set to zero). Appendix B Proof of Lemma 7
In this appendix, we give the proof of Lemma 7. The proof follows from the techniques of Bricmont and Kupiainen [3] with some additional care, since we have a different profile function \varphi defined in (12), and since we give the explicit dependence of the bounds in terms of all the components of initial data. As mentioned early, the proof relies mainly on the understanding of the behavior of the kernel \mathcal{K}(s,\sigma,y,x) (see (19)). This behavior follows from a perturbation method around e^{(s-\sigma)\mathcal{L}}(y,s) , where the kernel of e^{t\mathcal{L}} is given by Mehler’s formula:
e^{t\mathcal{L}}(y,x)=\frac{e^{t}}{\sqrt{4\pi(1-e^{-t})}}exp\left[-\frac{(ye^{-t/2}-x)^{2}}{4(1-e^{-t})}\right].
(48)
By definition (19) of \mathcal{K} , we use a Feynman-Kac representation for \mathcal{K} :
\mathcal{K}(s,\sigma,y,x)=e^{(s-\sigma)\mathcal{L}}(y,x)\int d\mu_{yx}^{s-\sigma}(\omega)e^{\int_{0}^{s-\sigma}V(\omega(\tau),\sigma+\tau)d\tau},

where d\mu_{yx}^{s-\sigma} is the oscillator measure on the continuous paths \omega:[0,s-\sigma]\to\mathbb{R} with \omega(0)=x , \omega(s-\sigma)=y , i.e. the Gaussian probability measure with covariance kernel

\displaystyle=\omega_{0}(\tau)\omega_{0}(\tau^{\prime})
\displaystyle+2\left(e^{-\frac{1}{2}|\tau-\tau^{\prime}|}-e^{-\frac{1}{2}|\tau+\tau^{\prime}|}+e^{-\frac{1}{2}|2(s-\sigma)+\tau-\tau^{\prime}|}-e^{-\frac{1}{2}|2(s-\sigma)-\tau-\tau^{\prime}|}\right),
which yields \int d\mu_{yx}^{s-\sigma}\omega(\tau)=\omega_{0}(\tau) , with
\omega_{0}(\tau)=\left(\sinh((s-\sigma)/2)\right)^{-1}\left(y\sinh(\frac{\tau}{2})+x\sinh(\frac{s-\sigma-\tau}{2})\right).

Lemma B.1 (Estimates on the potential V ).

|B_{m}(\tau)|=\left|\int\chi(\tau)B(q(\tau))k_{m}\rho dy\right|\leq\frac{CA^{4}}{\tau^{2+2\nu}}.
(59)
Since B_{-}(y,\tau)=\chi(\tau)B(q(\tau))-\sum_{m=0}^{2}B_{m}(\tau)h_{m}(y) , we have from (58) and (59),
\displaystyle\left|\frac{B_{-}(y,\tau)}{1+|y|^{3}}\right|
\displaystyle\leq\left|\frac{\chi(\tau)B(q(\tau))}{1+|y|^{3}}\right|+\left|\frac{\sum_{m=0}^{2}B_{m}(\tau)h_{m}(y)}{1+|y|^{3}}\right|
\displaystyle\leq\chi(\tau)\left[\frac{CA^{4}}{\tau^{3+2\varrho}}(1+|y|^{3})+\frac{CA^{4}}{\tau^{2+2\nu}}(1+|y|)\right]+\frac{CA^{4}}{\tau^{2+2\nu}}\left(\frac{|\sum_{m=0}^{2}h_{m}(y)|}{1+|y|^{3}}\right)
If we use |y|^{l}\chi(y,\tau)\leq C\tau^{l/2} for l\in\mathbb{N} , and |\sum_{m=0}^{2}h_{m}(y)|\leq C(1+|y|^{2}) , then we obtain
\left\|\frac{B_{-}(y,\tau)}{1+|y|^{3}}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\frac{CA^{4}}{\tau^{3/2+2\varrho}}.
Using the second estimates in (57) and (26), we obviously obtain \|B(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\frac{CA^{2p^{\prime}}}{\tau^{\varrho p^{\prime}}} which yields \|B_{e}(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\frac{CA^{2p^{\prime}}}{\tau^{\varrho p^{\prime}}} . This ends the proof of part i) .
ii) From the definition (16) of R , we write \varphi(y,\tau)=\frac{\phi(\tau)}{\kappa}\vartheta(y,\tau) and R(y,\tau)=\frac{\phi(\tau)}{\kappa}Q+G , where \vartheta(y,\tau)=f(\frac{y}{\sqrt{\tau}})+\frac{\kappa}{2p\tau} and
\displaystyle Q(y,\tau)
\displaystyle=-\vartheta_{\tau}+\Delta\vartheta-\frac{y}{2}\nabla\vartheta-\frac{\vartheta}{p-1}+\vartheta^{p},
(60)
\displaystyle G(y,\tau)
\displaystyle=-\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{\kappa}\vartheta-\frac{\phi}{\kappa}\vartheta^{p}+\phi^{p}\left(\frac{\vartheta}{\kappa}\right)^{p}+e^{\frac{-p\tau}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}\frac{\phi}{\kappa}\vartheta\right).
(61)
The conclusion of part ii) is a direct consequence of the following:
Lemma C.1.
There exists \sigma_{7}>0 such that for all \tau\geq\sigma_{7} , we have
i) (Estimates on Q )
\displaystyle m=0,1,\;
\displaystyle|Q_{m}(\tau)|\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{2}},\quad|Q_{2}(\tau)|\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{3}},
\displaystyle\left\|\frac{Q_{-}(y,\tau)}{1+|y|^{3}}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{2}},\quad\|Q_{e}(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\frac{C}{\sqrt{\tau}}.
(62)
ii) (Estimates on G )
m=0,1,2,\;|G_{m}(\tau)|\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{1+a^{\prime}}},\;\left\|\frac{G_{-}(y,\tau)}{1+|y|^{3}}\right\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{1+a^{\prime}}},\;\|G_{e}(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{a}},
(63)
where a^{\prime}=a>1 in the case (2) and a^{\prime}=a+1>1 in the case (3).
Proof.
i) See page 563 in [3]. For part ii) , one can see that it is a direct consequence of the following:
|G(y,\tau)|\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{a}}\quad\text{and}\quad|\chi(\tau)G(y,\tau)|\leq\frac{C}{\tau^{1+a^{\prime}}}(1+|y|^{2}).
(64)
By the definition of G_{m},G_{-} and G_{e} , part ii) simply follows from (64). By the linearity, this also concludes the proof of part ii) of Lemma 9.
Let us now give the proof of (64). For the first estimate, we use the definition (61) of G , Lemmas A.1 and A.2,
\displaystyle|G(y,\tau)|\leq\left|\frac{\phi^{\prime}\vartheta}{\kappa}\right|+\left|\frac{\phi\vartheta}{\kappa}\right|\left|1-\frac{\phi^{p-1}}{\kappa^{p-1}}\right|+\left|e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\frac{\phi\vartheta}{\kappa}\right)\right|\leq\frac{C}{s^{a}}.
For the second estimate in (64), we use the fact that \phi satisfies (6) and write
\displaystyle G(y,\tau)
\displaystyle=\frac{\vartheta\phi}{\kappa^{p}}(\kappa^{p-1}-\phi^{p-1})(\kappa^{p-1}-\vartheta^{p-1})
\displaystyle+e^{-\frac{p\tau}{p-1}}\left[h\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}\frac{\phi\vartheta}{\kappa}\right)-h\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}\phi\right)\right]
\displaystyle+\left(1-\frac{\vartheta}{\kappa}\right)e^{-\frac{p\tau}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}\phi\right):=\bar{G}+\tilde{G}+\hat{G}.
Noting that \vartheta(y,\tau)=\kappa\left(1-\frac{h_{2}(y)}{4p\tau}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{|y|^{4}}{\tau^{2}}\right)\right) uniformly for y\in\mathbb{R} and \tau\geq 1 , and recalling from Lemma A.2 that \phi(\tau)=\kappa(1+\eta_{a}(\tau))^{-\frac{1}{p-1}} where \eta_{a}(\tau)=\mathcal{O}(\tau^{-a}) , then using a Taylor expansion, we derive
\displaystyle\bar{G}(y,\tau)
\displaystyle=\frac{\phi\eta_{a}(\tau)}{1+\eta_{a}(\tau)}\left(\frac{h_{2}(y)}{4p\tau}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{|y|^{4}}{\tau^{2}}\right)\right),
\displaystyle\tilde{G}(y,\tau)
\displaystyle=-\phi e^{-\tau}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}\phi\right)\left(\frac{h_{2}(y)}{4p\tau}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{|y|^{4}}{\tau^{2}}\right)\right),
\displaystyle\hat{G}(y,\tau)
\displaystyle=e^{-\frac{p\tau}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}\phi\right)\left(\frac{h_{2}(y)}{4p\tau}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{|y|^{4}}{\tau^{2}}\right)\right).
This yields the second estimate in (64) in the case (2). If h is given by (3), we have furthermore
\displaystyle\left|\frac{\phi\eta_{a}(\tau)}{1+\eta_{a}(\tau)}-e^{-s}h^{\prime}(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi)\phi+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi)\right|
\displaystyle\leq\left|\frac{\phi}{1+\eta_{a}(\tau)}\right|\left|\eta_{a}(\tau)-\frac{\mu}{\log^{a}\left(2+e^{\frac{2\tau}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(\tau)\right)}\right|+\frac{C}{\tau^{a+1}}\leq\frac{2C}{\tau^{1+a}},
which yields the second estimate in (64) in the case (3). This concludes the proof of (64) and the proof of part ii) of Lemma 9 also.
∎
iii) From the definition (17) of N , we use a Taylor expansion for N to find that in the case (2),
N(q(\tau),\tau)=e^{-\tau}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}(\phi(\tau)+\theta_{1}q(\tau))\right)q(\tau)\quad\text{with}\quad\theta_{1}\in[0,1],
and in the case (3),
N(q(\tau),\tau)=e^{-\frac{(p-2)\tau}{p-1}}h^{\prime\prime}\left(e^{\frac{\tau}{p-1}}(\phi(\tau)+\theta_{2}q(\tau))\right)q^{2}(\tau)\quad\text{with}\quad\theta_{2}\in[0,1].
Since \varphi(\tau)\to\kappa and \|q(\tau)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})}\to 0 as \tau\to+\infty , this implies that there exists \tau_{0} large enough such that \frac{\kappa}{2}\leq|\phi(\tau)+\theta_{i}q(\tau)|\leq\frac{3\kappa}{2} for all \tau\geq\tau_{0} and y\in\mathbb{R} . Then by Lemma A.1, we have |N(q(\tau),\tau)|\leq\frac{C|q|^{\beta}}{\tau^{a}} where \beta=1 in the case (2) and \beta=2 in the case (3), which implies part iii) of Lemma 9. This concludes the proof of Lemma 9.
∎
References
[1]
J. M. Ball.
Remarks on blow-up and nonexistence theorems for nonlinear evolution
equations.
Quart. J. Math. Oxford Ser. (2), 28(112):473–486, 1977.

label: nguyen-ode-v4.txt-47
purpose: earlier companion PDE requires logarithmic exponent greater than one
text:
We are interested in the following nonlinear parabolic equation:
\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}&=&\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u+h(u),\\
u(0)&=&u_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\end{array}\right.
(1)
where u is defined for (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T) , p is a sub-critical nonlinearity,
1<p,\quad(n-2)p<n+2.
(2)
The function h is in \mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) satisfying
j=0,1,\;|h^{(j)}(z)|\leq M\left(\dfrac{|z|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}+1\right),\quad|h^{\prime\prime}(z)|\leq M\dfrac{|z|^{p-2}}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})},
(3)
where a>1 , M>0 . Typically, h(z)=\frac{\mu|z|^{p-1}z}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})} with \mu\in\mathbb{R} .
By standard results, the problem (1) has a unique classical solution u(x,t) in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}) , which exists at least for small times. The solution u(x,t) may develop singularities in some finite time. We say that a function u:\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,T)\mapsto\mathbb{R} is a solution of (1) if u solves (1) and satisfies
u,u_{t},\nabla u,\nabla^{2}u\;\text{are bounded and continuous on}\;\mathbb{R}^{n}\times[0,\tau],\;\forall\tau<T.
(4)
It is said that u(x,t) blows up in a finite time T<+\infty if u(x,t) satisfies (1), (4) and
\lim_{t\to T}\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}=+\infty.
Here we call T the blow-up time of u(x,t) . In such a blow-up case, a point x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is called a blow-up point of u(x,t) if and only if there exist (x_{n},t_{n})\to(x_{0},T) such that |u(x_{n},t_{n})|\to+\infty as n\to+\infty .

label: nguyen-ode-v4.txt-966
purpose: full antecedent amplitude ODE proof, Lemmas A.1–A.3
text:
Appendix A Appendix A
The following lemma shows the asymptotic behavior of the solution of the associated ODE of equation 1:
Lemma A.1.
Let v be a blow-up solution of the following ordinary differential equation:
v^{\prime}(t)=v^{p}(t)+h(v),\quad v(T)=+\infty\quad\text{for some $T>0$},
(94)
where h is defined in (3). Then v satisfies
v(t)\sim\kappa(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\quad\text{as $t\to T$, where $\kappa=(p-1)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}$}.
Proof.
Divide (94) by v^{p} and note that \frac{h(v)}{v^{p}}\to 0 as v\to+\infty , we see that for all \varepsilon>0 , there exists a number \delta=\delta(\epsilon)>0 such that
\left|\frac{v^{\prime}}{v^{p}}-1\right|\leq\varepsilon,\quad\forall t\in[T-\delta,T).
(95)
Solving (95) with noting that v(T)=+\infty yields
\displaystyle(1+\varepsilon)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\kappa(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}
\displaystyle\leq v(t)\leq(1-\varepsilon)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\kappa(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad\forall t\in[T-\delta,T).
This concludes the proof of Lemma A.1.
∎
The following lemma gives us an estimation of the perturbation term in equation (9):
Lemma A.2.
Let h be the function defined in (3), then it holds that
j=0,1,\quad e^{-\frac{(p-j)s}{p-1}}\left|h^{(j)}\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}w\right)\right|\leq Cs^{-a}\left(|w|^{p-j}+1\right),\quad\forall s\geq\hat{s},
where C=C(a,p,\mu,M)>0 and \hat{s}=\hat{s}(a,p)>0 such that \frac{\log s}{s}\leq\frac{p}{a(p-1)} for all s\geq\hat{s} .
Proof.
We have from (3) that for j=0,1,
e^{-\frac{(p-j)s}{p-1}}\left|h^{(j)}\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}w\right)\right|\leq C^{\prime}(M,\mu)\left(\frac{|w|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}\left(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}w^{2}\right)}+e^{-\frac{(p-j)s}{p-1}}\right).
Considering the first case w^{2}e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\geq 4 , we have
\frac{|w|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}\left(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}w^{2}\right)}\leq\frac{|w|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}\left(4e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\right)}\leq\frac{(p-1)^{a}}{s^{a}}|w|^{p-j}.
Now, considering the second case w^{2}e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\leq 4 , we have |w|^{p-j}\leq 2^{p-j}e^{-\frac{(p-j)s}{2(p-1)}} which yields
\frac{|w|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}\left(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}w^{2}\right)}\leq\frac{|w|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}(2)}\leq\frac{2^{p-j}}{\log^{a}2}e^{-\frac{(p-j)s}{2(p-1)}}.
Taking C=\max\left\{C^{\prime},\frac{2^{p}}{\log^{a}2},(p-1)^{a}\right\} and \hat{s}>0 such that e^{-\frac{(p-j)s}{p-1}}\leq s^{-a} for all s\geq\hat{s} , we have the conclusion. This ends the proof of Lemma A.2.
∎
The following lemma shows us the existence of solutions of the associated ODE of equation (9):
Lemma A.3.
Let \phi be a positive solution of the following ordinary differential equation:
\phi_{s}=-\frac{\phi}{p-1}+\phi^{p}+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi\right).
(96)
Then \phi(s)\to\kappa as s\to+\infty and \phi(s) is given by
\phi(s)=\kappa(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad\text{where}\quad\eta_{a}(s)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a}}\right).
(97)
If h(x)=\mu\frac{|x|^{p-1}x}{\log^{a}(2+x^{2})} , we have
\eta_{a}(s)\sim C_{0}\int_{s}^{+\infty}\frac{e^{s-\tau}}{\tau^{a}}d\tau=\frac{C_{0}}{s^{a}}\left(1+\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{b_{j}}{s^{j}}\right),
where C_{0}=\mu\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)^{a} and b_{j}=(-1)^{j}\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(a+i) .
Proof.
By the following transformation
v(t)=(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\phi(s),\quad s=-\log(T-t),
equation (94) is transformed into (96). From Lemma A.1, we see that \phi(s)\to\kappa as s\to+\infty .
By dividing equation (96) by \phi^{p} , we find that
\left(\frac{1}{\phi^{p-1}}\right)^{\prime}=\frac{1}{\phi^{p-1}}-(p-1)(1+g(s)),\quad g(s)=\frac{1}{\phi^{p}}e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi\right).
(98)
Since \phi(s)\to\kappa as s\to+\infty , we have from Lemma A.2 that g(s)=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a}}\right) as s\to+\infty . Solving equation (98) yields
\phi(s)=\kappa\left(1+\eta_{a}(s)\right)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad\text{where}\quad\eta_{a}(s)=\int_{s}^{+\infty}e^{s-\tau}g(\tau)d\tau.
By integration by part, we find that
\int_{s}^{+\infty}e^{s-\tau}\tau^{-a}d\tau=\frac{1}{s^{a}}\left(1+\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{b_{j}}{s^{j}}\right),\quad b_{j}=(-1)^{j}\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(a+i).
(99)
This follows that \eta_{a}(s)=\mathcal{O}(s^{-a}) as s\to+\infty . In particular case h(x)=\mu\frac{|x|^{p-1}x}{\log^{a}(2+x^{2})} , we have g(s)=\mu\log^{-a}\left(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(s)\right)\sim\mu\left(\frac{p-1}{2s}\right)^{a} as s\to+\infty . By (99), we get the desired result and finish the proof of Lemma A.3.
∎

label: nguyen-analysis-v1.txt-649
purpose: later companion repeats amplitude lemma and cancellation
text:
Appendix A Appendix A
The following lemma from [32] gives the expansion of \phi(s) , the unique solution of equation (18) satisfying (19):
Lemma A.1.
Let \phi be a positive solution of the following ordinary differential equation:
\phi_{s}=-\frac{\phi}{p-1}+\phi^{p}+\frac{\mu\phi^{p}}{\log^{a}(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2})}.
Assuming in addition \phi(s)\to\kappa as s\to+\infty , then \phi(s) takes the following form:
\phi(s)=\kappa(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty,
where
\eta_{a}(s)\sim C_{*}\int_{s}^{+\infty}\frac{e^{s-\tau}}{\tau^{a}}d\tau=\frac{C_{*}}{s^{a}}\left(1+\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{b_{j}}{s^{j}}\right),
with C_{*}=\mu\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)^{a} and b_{j}=(-1)^{j}\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(a+i) .
Proof.
See Lemma A.3 in [32].
∎
Appendix B Appendix B
We aim at proving the following:
Lemma B.1 (Estimate of \omega(s) ).
We have
|\omega(s)|=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}\right),\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty.
Proof.
From Lemma A.1, we write
p(\phi(s)^{p-1}-\kappa^{p-1})=-\frac{p\eta_{a}(s)}{p-1}(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-1}=-\frac{pC_{*}}{(p-1)s^{a}}(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-1}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}\right).
A direct calculation yields,
\displaystyle e^{-s}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{p}{p-1}}\phi(s)\right)
\displaystyle=\frac{\mu p\phi^{p-1}(s)}{\log^{a}(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(s))}-\frac{2a\mu e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{p+1}(s)}{(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(s))\log^{a+1}(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(s))}
\displaystyle=\frac{pC_{*}}{(p-1)s^{a}}(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-1}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}\right).
Adding the two above estimates, we obtain the desired result. This ends the proof of Lemma B.1.
∎
Lemma B.2 (Estimate of R(y,s) ).
We have
|R(y,s)|=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{|y|^{2}+1}{s^{a^{\prime}+1}}\right),\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty,
with a^{\prime}=\min\{1,a\} .
Proof.
Let us write \varphi(y,s)=\frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa}\nu(y,s) where
\nu(y,s)=\kappa\left(1+\frac{p-1}{4ps}\sum_{j=1}^{l}y_{j}^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}+\frac{\kappa l}{2ps}.
Then, we write R(y,s)=\frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa}R_{1}(y,s)+R_{2}(y,s) where
\displaystyle R_{1}(y,s)
\displaystyle=\nu_{s}-\Delta\nu-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla\nu-\frac{\nu}{p-1}+\nu^{p},
\displaystyle R_{2}(y,s)
\displaystyle=-\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{\kappa}\nu-\frac{\phi}{\kappa}\nu^{p}+\phi^{p}\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)^{p}+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\frac{\phi\nu}{\kappa}\right).
The term R_{1}(y,s) is already treated in [34], and it is bounded by
|R_{1}(y,s)|\leq\frac{C(|y|^{2}+1)}{s^{2}}+C\mathbf{1}_{\{|y|\geq 2K_{0}\sqrt{s}\}}.
To bound R_{2} , we use the fact that \phi satisfies (19) to write
\displaystyle R_{2}(y,s)
\displaystyle=\frac{\nu\phi}{\kappa^{p}}(\kappa^{p-1}-\phi^{p-1})(\kappa^{p-1}-\nu^{p-1})
\displaystyle+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}\left[h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\frac{\phi\nu}{\kappa}\right)-h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi\right)\right]
\displaystyle+\left(1-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi\right).
Noting that \nu(y,s)=\kappa+\bar{\nu}(y,s) with |\bar{\nu}(y,s)|\leq\frac{C}{s}(|y|^{2}+1) , uniformly for y\in\mathbb{R} and s\geq 1 , and recalling from Lemma A.1 that \phi(s)=\kappa(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-\frac{1}{p-1}} where \eta_{a}(s)=\mathcal{O}(s^{-a}) , then using a Taylor expansion, we derive
|R_{2}(y,s)|\leq C\left(\frac{|y|^{2}+1}{s^{a+1}}+\mathbf{1}_{\{|y|\geq 2K_{0}\sqrt{s}\}}\right).
This concludes the proof of Lemma B.2.
∎
